I have been working on a version of this for a while - in the form of reification - representing the function body as value.

The design: if a function accepts a Code(f) argument, you can pass finto it, where f is a type of any pure Roc function expression. The compiler passes into this argument a Typed AST value that can be translated as necessary within Roc. The function passed can be polymorphic, and the types inside are resolved just like they would in a normal function call site. What you translate the AST into is your business - could be strings for SQL, could be effectful platform calls.

It is beautiful IMO, it unlocks various DSLs that have no syntax overhead - imagine:

  # main.roc: the rows are ordinary records, the clauses ordinary Roc functions
  Product : { id : I64, title : Str, price : Dec }

  products : Sql.Table(Product)
  products = Sql.table("products")

  is_premium : Product -> Bool
  is_premium = |p| p.price >= 20

  expect is_premium({ id: 1, title: "Espresso machine", price: 249 })

  premium : Try(Str, Sql.Error)
  premium = Sql.from(products).filter(is_premium).select(|p| { title: p.title }).to_sql()
  # Ok("SELECT products.title AS title\nFROM products\nWHERE (products.price >= 20.0)")

Notice how transforms and predicates are pure Roc and operate on plain Roc struct, yet the result is domain-specific.

Since there's this discussion, I'll publish the prototype in a couple of days - there are some features I wanted to polish first.

line_total : Order, Product -> Dec
line_total = |order, product| product.price * order.quantity.to_dec() * (1 - order.discount)

expect line_total({ id: 1, customer_id: 1, product_id: 1, quantity: 4, discount: 0.25 }, { id: 1, title: "Pen", price: 2.50 }) == 7.5

report_line = |((c, o), p)| { customer: c.name, product: p.title, quantity: o.quantity, total: line_total(o, p) }

purchases =
    Sql.from(customers)
        .join(orders, |c, o| o.customer_id == c.id)
        .join(products, |(_, o), p| o.product_id == p.id)

bulk_lines =
    purchases
        .filter(bulk_purchase)
        .select(report_line)
        .order_by(|r| r.total, Desc)

This design only introduces the tag union that describes pure roc and the Code(f) rule for arguments - no new syntax.

Isn't solvable with a fluent builder interface? Literally this same syntax, but just using normal Roc values, instead of analysing the function body.

If I write something in this DSL, how do I know that it is not going to run like normal Roc code? The behavior is different than if it were running as Roc, and I guess the type inference is also different.

The types are inferred based on the usual Roc rules - the question is how these types are translated. The idea is the Translator function preserves the semantics of the type - e.g. uses the correct implementation for integer and float divisions, uses appropriate target types for u32 and u64 Roc values etc. This is a pretty basic expectation IMO - if a translator does not respect Roc types it is malformed. I imagine most translators won't implement all types abd primitives; in this case the translator rejects the AST node, and the user gets a nice error with clear code location

notramo said:

Isn't solvable with a fluent builder interface?

This isn't about the builder pattern, that is just for showcase. It's about the functions that, in this example, get passed into builder methods - they are plain Roc. Some of this UX can be achieved with Static Dispatch, but it doesn't come close - the most obvious example are and and or - the static dispatch can't overload these because they have to return Bool. And the code that uses Static Dispatch wraps everything in custom types that don't work directly with plain Roc

notramo said:

Ihow do I know that it is not going to run like normal Roc code?

In the current design this is encoded in the functions you call - in the above examples you just know that .select, .join, .filter reify (because of Code(a) in their type signature), because you are using this SQL DSL package based on reifying.

You could wrap the code that you want to reify with e.g. .filter(reify_code(is_premium)) , but I think it defeats the ergonomics benefits.

To be clear, the code that gets reified is not DSL - it is Roc - the DSL is the function that reifies it. The semantics you express are the Roc semantics, and a well-written DSL (that uses translators that process the AST, resulting from reification) should respect them.

It is not a novel idea - there are similar features in C# (System.Linq.Expressions) and Julia (Quoting), and reification is considered a great feature in both.
Often reification has downsides like loss of types or patchy language coverage, but the beauty of Roc's type system allows for strict typing through-and-through and a clean boundary - all pure Roc (whose types can be fully resolved at the call site) being supported for reifying.

Basically, only the substitution happens when the function expression is passed into a matching Code(a) slot - no explicit Code(value) call - Code stays type-level.
In the example filter has type filter : Query(row), Code(row -> Bool) -> Query(row), where Query is the usual Roc type that hosts the builder pattern methods and "state".

is_premium's Product fits into the polymorphic slot of the Code(row -> Bool) type, so is accepted and reified into the typed AST - every field name, value type etc. is known - resolved as in a simple Roc call.

The AST is not translated "back" to Roc. The "Translator" - the Roc code that received the Code(a) value and matches/processes the recursive AST tag union - builds whatever representation it wants, or, again, does some effectful calls if it needs to, making the return value a Task. There is no mechanism to get the compiled Roc back from the reified value. You can of course call the function you reify in one place normally in a different place - the reification happens at call site of the reifier function (that triggers the reifying because of the Code in it's type declaration), with types resolved there.
You could pass some toInt : a -> I32 into Code(Str -> a) and have that resolved correctly, and turned into the AST.

No, in this case it's simply a translator : Code(a) -> Task whatever. You just get an AST value and do what you want with it

I do not have expertise in language design, but Roc's type inference seems like a great feature to leverage for DSLs - you can have concise code with minimal boilerplate, yet expressive and strongly typed.

so in c# a great use case for this is something like a query builder

var post = dbContext.Posts; // this is IQueryble, so for example Filter takes the Expression<...> which is the "code as structs", auto converter

if(request.HideArchived){
   posts = posts.Where( x => x.IsArchived); // this get accumulated
}

if(!request.TitleFilter.IsNullOrEmpty())
{
    posts = posts.Where(x => x.Title.Contains(request.TitleFilter, Comparison.InvariantCultureCaseInsensitive);
}

return posts.Select(post => new { id = post.Id,  title = post.Title, commnetCount = post.Comments.Count()});

this will produce a VERY good SQL, of course tailored to whatever database provider you are using, whether it's SQLite or Snowflake. The Contains will be translated to something like where title ilike '%{:title}%' (syntax from memory for postgres, so probably not that accurate), multiple Where will become an and. You get the idea :) these days you rarely have to fix that, unless you do something really weird.

There are some functions that don't do anyting in C#, but map to SQL, for example:

posts.Where( post => EF.Functions.Like(post.Name, "%smith"))

With Roc I imagine you can have this verified at compile time whether all the code you used in there actually can be mapped to SQL

For example:

bool IsRecentlyArchived(Post p) => p.IsArchived && p.ArchiveDate > DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-7);

posts.Where(IsRecentlyArchived); // this is ok, even the DateTime.UtcNow will be translated to a db instruction

posts.Where(p => p.Author == "someone" && IsRecentlyArchived(p)) // this fails on runtime

post.Where(p => p.Author == "someone").Where(IsRecentlyArchived) // this is fine

thing is, for GraphQL this can be really nicely generate in runtime and cover so many cases

No. Because it's a string. It's obvious that the Roc syntax constructs are not applied inside strings, because strings are opaque to Roc type system and control flow.

comp time reading AST nodes in userspace is a huge downside. It means you can no longer look at a snippet of Roc code and even have confidence that you understand basic properties like what the control flow is anymore. Anything could mean anything.
macros have the same downside, and I've had a longstanding goal of never putting macros in the language - this is one reason why.

writing AST nodes is less of a downside but I'm not really sure what the benefit of that would be compared to normal function composition. It sounds like a solution in search of a problem but maybe I'm missing something.

so a quick comparison with EF Core:

The function names are the same in EF, so you have select for Surreal, and map for normal Roc collections

Cool trick in EF is that you can easily convert the IEnumerable (that would be Iter in Roc) to IQueryable (which uses Expression<Func<_>>, so reification, while IEnumerable takes normal Func<_>), so can have have a single function that operates on both.

another thing is that like in your case, the queries are lazy, so the database trip happens exacty where you think it is. In your code it's bind(), in EF it's .ToListAsync() or for foreach(var pattient in dbContext.Patients.Where(x => x.Name.Contains("Steve"))

So, iterating the query triggers it. You can even make it query.ToAsyncEnumerable() which would give you something like Roc Stream, and a buffered read, so you can foreach over millions of rows as long as 2 or 3 fit in memory at once.

You can also do dbContext.Patients.Where(x => x.Name.Contains("Steve").ToAsyncEnumerable().Where(x => x.Id %2) - the first Where will happen in the database, the second at runtime in C#.

Also, defining the tables is a bit funny in your example, they seem to float around as global objects (you picked quite a domain to show this off), in EF you define a DbContext that has properties of type DbSet<SomeClass> and every type that is reachable from there will become a database table (unless configured as Owned type or JSON column)

EF also does change tracking, but since we are working with immutable structures, that should not be a thing - and that's great actually

I am also not sure how you designed your links, but in EF if there is a link to another table, by default it's not loaded unless use it in your query
